message.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    We analyze the phases of theories having a microscopic
                    <a:math xmlns:a="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <a:msub>
                        <a:mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</a:mi>
                        <a:mi>N</a:mi>
                      </a:msub>
                    </a:math>
                    1-form symmetry, starting with a topological  theory and deforming it so that only the microscopic symmetry is preserved. These theories have a well-defined notion of confinement, prototypical examples being pure
                    <d:math xmlns:d="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <d:mi>SU</d:mi>
                      <d:mo stretchy="false">(</d:mo>
                      <d:mi>N</d:mi>
                      <d:mo stretchy="false">)</d:mo>
                    </d:math>
                    and
                    <h:math xmlns:h="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <h:msub>
                        <h:mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</h:mi>
                        <h:mi>N</h:mi>
                      </h:msub>
                    </h:math>
                    gauge theories in the continuum and on the lattice. Our analysis shows that the generic phases are in
                    <k:math xmlns:k="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <k:mi>d</k:mi>
                      <k:mo>=</k:mo>
                      <k:mn>2</k:mn>
                    </k:math>
                    , only the confined phase; in
                    <m:math xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <m:mi>d</m:mi>
                      <m:mo>=</m:mo>
                      <m:mn>3</m:mn>
                    </m:math>
                    , both the confined phase and the topological  phase; and in
                    <o:math xmlns:o="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <o:mi>d</o:mi>
                      <o:mo>=</o:mo>
                      <o:mn>4</o:mn>
                    </o:math>
                    , the confined phase, the topological  phase, and a Coulomb phase. We construct a
                    <q:math xmlns:q="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <q:msub>
                        <q:mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</q:mi>
                        <q:mi>N</q:mi>
                      </q:msub>
                    </q:math>
                    lattice gauge theory with a deformation that, surprisingly, produces up to (
                    <t:math xmlns:t="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <t:mrow>
                        <t:mi>N</t:mi>
                        <t:mo>−</t:mo>
                        <t:mn>1</t:mn>
                      </t:mrow>
                    </t:math>
                    ) photons. We give an interpretation of these findings in terms of the behaviors of two competing drivers of confinement—magnetic monopoles and center vortices—and conclude that proliferation of center vortices is necessary but insufficient for confinement, while proliferation of magnetic monopoles is both necessary and sufficient.
                  </jats:p>
title:
Phases of Theories with
                    <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <mml:mrow>
                        <mml:msub>
                          <mml:mrow>
                            <mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mml:mi>
                          </mml:mrow>
                          <mml:mrow>
                            <mml:mi>N</mml:mi>
                          </mml:mrow>
                        </mml:msub>
                      </mml:mrow>
                    </mml:math>
                    1-Form Symmetry, and the Roles of Center Vortices and Magnetic Monopoles

reference.unstructured: This is not to say that confinement has no meaning in theories with fundamental matter such as QCD—a perspective which is sometimes conflated with the absence of 1-form symmetry. Confinement in QCD is the statement that there are no asymptotic quark states.
For instance, pure SU(N) gauge theory can be deformed by introducing two adjoint scalars which may Higgs SU(N) to ZN.
This association is also sometimes made on the lattice; see, e.g., Ref. [28].

See Supplemental Material at http://link.aps.org/supplemental/10.1103/PhysRevLett.134.141902 for further discussion on (1) BF theory, (2) 2D confinement, (3) 3D ZN lattice gauge theory, (4) center vortex contributions to Wilson loop averages, and (5) multiflavor photon phases in 4D, which includes Refs. [30–34].
G[p] denotes a p-form symmetry group G.
Related observations have been made in many works including [1, 20, 37, 38, 39, 40].

reference.volume-title: NATO Advanced Research Workshop on Theoretical Physics: New Developments in Quantum Field Theory
reference.author: L. Del Debbio

reference.unstructured: Kinetic terms for all fields are always generated. While they are irrelevant relative to the BF term, being higher in derivatives, we include them because they can be dangerously irrelevant.

The emergence of 1-form symmetry is a subtle issue, but Ref. [44] points out that it is robust when the would-be emergent symmetry spontaneously breaks or participates in a mixed anomaly, as is the case here and everywhere else we speak of emergent 1-form symmetry.
l,p,c, denote oriented links, plaquettes, and cubes. For variables vσr on r cells σr, we write (dv)σr+1≡∑σr∈∂σr+1vσr, with the understanding that v−σr=−vσr.
The dual of an r cell σr in the original lattice, denoted *σr, is the unique (d−r) cell in the dual lattice that intersects σr at a point. The dual of a cell in the dual lattice is similarly defined.

In the Villain formulation, the term μ∑|dm|2 may be exactly dualized to a term proportional to μ−1∑|dχ˜+2πs˜+a˜|2, where χ˜ is a continuous field on dual sites and s˜ is an integer field on dual links.
